deeper.title: What the price assumes
deeper.text: The price assumes about 34% a year growth in free cash flow for 10 years, then 3% (discount rate 10.1% = 10-year Treasury 5.1% + 5%; base: sales × its 3-year median free-cash margin (3%), because current free cash flow is negative). For comparison, sales grew 15% last year; 13%/yr over 3 years — the market expects faster growth than the company has recently delivered.

deeper.title: Return on capital
deeper.text: 12% (3 years ago 12%, about the same) — each $100 invested in the business (debt + equity, net of cash) earns about $12 a year after tax; return on shareholders' equity 22% (3 years ago 11%).

deeper.title: Signed future revenue
deeper.text: Customer prepayments not yet earned (deferred revenue): $28.2B, up 12% from a year ago.

deeper.title: Earnings-quality red flags
flags: Receivables (money customers still owe) up 61% vs quarterly sales up 12% (days to collect 31 → 44). Customers may be paying more slowly, or sales were pulled forward.

deeper.title: Multi-year view
deeper.text: Sales grew 13%/yr over 3 years and 12%/yr over 5 years; operating margin today 13% vs a 5-year range of 2–13% (median 9%): near the top of its range (cycle peak risk: margins this high often fall back).

deeper.title: Cash returned to shareholders

summary.act_at: Consider buying near 251.93–257.04 support; fuller value at 238.65

note.happening: Amazon closed at 266.66, down 0.29% on the day. That is just above 266.4, the top of its own-history value range. The price has moved sideways, and its 20-, 50- and 200-day averages are all flat. The only news since the last note is a reported discount on a third-party speaker sold on the platform, which has no bearing on the business. No earnings date is in the data.
note.business: Things that change the business: the latest quarter's sales grew 12.09% from a year earlier, down from 16.61% two quarters ago, so growth is slowing. Profitability is improving. Operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, rose to 13.09% from 11.02%. Cash is going the wrong way. Free cash flow, the cash left after spending on the business, was -46.9B over the last 12 months against 10.6B a year before. Debt of 180.9B exceeds cash of 55.8B, leaving net debt of 66.7B, though 114.2B of available liquidity means funding is not under strain. The filings flag unpaid customer bills up 61% while quarterly sales grew 12%. That can mean sales were pulled forward or that customers are paying more slowly. Analysts cut their EPS estimate for next quarter by 2.6% over 30 days, to 2.3. Things that change only sentiment: the speaker headline and the general weakness in tech stocks. The cash position and the margin trend are the real questions. Amazon's ability to stay solvent and its market position (general knowledge) are not at risk.

worth.text: No cash-flow-based valuation (DCF) is possible here because free cash flow is negative. Our only method is Amazon's own history of price-to-sales, which is the share price divided by sales per share. At the 20th, 50th and 80th percentiles of the last 5 years, that gives 187.93, 238.65 and 266.4 per share. The price of 266.66 is just above the top. Price-to-sales is now at the 82nd percentile of Amazon's own 5-year range. The price is 21.6 times trailing earnings and 20.8 times this year's estimate. It is 25.0 times next year's estimate, because analysts expect lower next-year EPS of 10.67 against 12.8 this year. Compared with peers, the stock looks cheaper. Its price-to-sales of 3.6 is below the peer median of 6.6, and on a growth-adjusted basis it trades at 0.62 of peers. That gap explains the difference between the two views: Amazon looks expensive against its own past and cheap against its peers. The filings estimate that the price needs about 34% yearly growth, while Amazon delivered 13% a year over 3 years.
worth.key_assumption: Amazon's price-to-sales stays within its own 5-year range rather than moving toward the peer median of 6.6.
